Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SRE); Samir Patel (Polaris Head of ML), Laura Kim (Infra Lead), Carlos Mendes (Product), Nadia Olsen (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to run through tail-latency SLAs and how our autoscale fallback and priority queueing could help you hit the 95th/99th percentiles without overprovisioning. Quick round-robin intros?
[00:18] Samir (Polaris): Samir here, head of ML at Polaris. We're running a mix of synchronous route optimization queries and async batch ingestion. Our SLA target is 95th <= 150ms and 99th <= 350ms for routing microcalls.
[00:32] Diego (Redwood SE): Got it. Quick note: that 99th tail is where a lot of folks either reserve capacity or lean on pre-warm strategies. We'll talk through fallback policies so you don't have to permanently reserve expensive GPUs for rare spikes.
[00:46] Laura (Polaris Infra): We're also constrained by VPC egress rules on our side and need an on-prem option for some routes. Can Redwood's private deploy support the same autoscale semantics?
[00:58] Priya (Redwood SRE): Yes, Private exposes the same runtime primitives: per-route concurrency limits, priority queues, and a local scaling controller. The only difference is the control-plane handshake for policy updates.
[01:12] Carlos (Product): Can you define priority queues? Do we get per-customer or per-route priorities?
[01:18] Diego: We support priority at route-level and token-level weighting. For Polaris you'd likely do route-level—routing queries are high-priority; background summarization is low. High-priority requests skip the bulk queue and get preemptive slot allocation.
[01:31] Nadia (Security): Quick security q: when a request is promoted, is metadata stored in logs? We need to ensure PII isn't leaked during debugging.
[01:38] Maya: Good call. We can redact request bodies in audit logs; only non-sensitive headers and routing tags are kept. We'll send the audit log schema after the call.
[01:45] 
[02:05] Diego: Let's talk queueing model. Polaris's trace will likely show a heavy head but a long tail of small bursts. Our priority queueing is a multi-level queue with preemptive dispatch for level 0 (critical) and token-bucket shaped admission for lower levels. In practice that means critical ops see consistent latency, and lower priority ops are throttled back.
[02:35] Samir: We have some weird microsecond spikes due to tokenization overhead when payloads vary. Any guidance?
[02:40] Diego: Yeah tokenization variance is a common tail cause. Two things—1) normalize input sizes on the client side where possible and 2) use prefix caching in the KV cache. If you have repeated prompts, warm the KV cache on preflight.
[02:56] Carlos: When you say "KV cache warmup", is that a separate call or baked into the runtime?
[03:02] Priya: We provide a warmup API that lets you populate KV slots for a specific model+version/hypers. Diego will demo the script. Note that warmup itself consumes capacity so we recommend running warmups during off-peak or as prewarm tasks tied to your deployment pipeline.
[03:18] Diego: I'll also add a lightweight k6 script that simulates your route distribution—this helps estimate how many prewarmed slots you need for a given 99th target.
[03:28] 
[03:45] Laura: Curious about autoscale fallback: if your main pool is saturated, do you fallback to a smaller model automatically?
[03:51] Diego: Yes, fallback policies can be chained. Example flow: full-capacity pool -> compatible quantized variant -> CPU-safe smaller model (or hosted fallback). Each fallback step defines an expected latency distribution and quality delta. You configure cost thresholds and quality tolerances.
[04:10] Samir: How do you measure quality delta programmatically? Our routing logic needs a threshold.
[04:15] Maya: We recommend using Redwood Optimize eval hooks—run a short A/B on your prompt set measuring ROUGE or custom scoring. Diego: we can help set up an automated regression alert when fallback triggers exceed X% of requests.
[04:30] 
[04:48] Diego: On the runtime side, tail latency is heavily influenced by batching windows and kernel selection. Our runtime uses continuous batching with adaptive windowing—if traffic is low, we don't wait to fill large batches; if traffic surges, we expand batching to maximize throughput without breaking latency SLOs.
[05:07] Priya: Kernel selection is dynamic; for quantized models we pick INT8 kernels when sequence length is shorter and fallback to FP16 for longer contexts where INT8 quality drops. That selection is per-shard and per-token budget aware.
[05:24] Carlos: Does quantization introduce extra latency due to dequantize steps?
[05:28] Diego: Minimal—most kernels do fused quant-dequant where possible. The more common latency hit is from cache misses in KV cache after model swaps. If you switch between full and quantized variants frequently, the cache might be invalidated or inefficient.
[05:45] Samir: So we need to plan for cache affinity per-model variant.
[05:48] Diego: Exactly. Best practice—pin high-priority routes to a single model variant and use a separate pool for background traffic. That reduces cross-variant cache churn.
[06:00] 
[06:18] Laura: For reserved GPUs—what's the recommended headroom? We don't want idle GPUs but need to hit 99th.
[06:24] Maya: Two approaches: a) reserved baseline sized for 95th and burst onto ephemeral/generic pools for the 99th, or b) reserved for 99th but use aggressive prewarm + KV cache to lower that baseline. We usually model using a Poisson/empirical arrival distribution. Diego can run a Monte Carlo sim once we have traces.
[06:46] Diego: If you give us a week of traces (even sampled), we can estimate the probability mass in the tail and recommend reserved counts and burst buffer sizes. It's often nonlinear—doubling reserved GPUs doesn't halve the 99th if your burst shape is heavy-tailed.
[07:02] Samir: That's what we suspected. We also have multi-tenant concerns: different customers with different SLOs. Can Redwood provide per-tenant priority shaping?
[07:10] Priya: Yes, per-tenant tags and token accounting lets you apply different admission and preemption. You can set hard SLAs for premium accounts and soft for others.
[07:20] Nadia: From compliance, we need audit trails when preemptions happen and which tenant caused the preemption. Is that available?
[07:26] Maya: Yes, preemption events are logged with routing tags but request payloads can be redacted. We'll add sample logs to the security packet.
[07:34] 
[07:50] Diego: Let's walk through a quick queueing sketch. Imagine a two-queue model: high-priority (HP) with capacity lambda_HP and best-effort queue (BE). HP uses preemptive slots: if a HP arrives and BE uses all regular slots, we evict a BE request only if it hasn't hit a safety threshold. Admissions are token-bucket rate-limited to prevent HP floods. The trick is choosing safety thresholds to bound tail latency without causing thrash.
[08:20] Samir: That safety threshold—can we tune it dynamically? Like base it on the current 95th estimate?
[08:25] Diego: Absolutely. Our controller exposes metrics and an adaptive threshold policy: when observed 95th moves above target, the controller tightens BE preemption windows or spins up extra capacity.
[08:36] Carlos: How about backpressure to clients? We want the client to know if a request will be queued long.
[08:41] Diego: We support a 202 Accepted style where we return a queue token and ETA, plus websocket updates if desired. For strict SLAs we recommend sync with preemptive slots, for less strict you can async them.
[08:53] 
[09:10] Laura: VPC/on-prem: network latency between customer infra and model hosting matters. For private deployments, do you recommend colocating the model on the same subnet as the API gateway?
[09:19] Priya: Yes, colocate as close as possible. For on-prem we package the inference runtime as a container with host networking to minimize hop counts. Also ensure your HSM/KMS is in-region to reduce crypto roundtrips for per-request decryption.
[09:33] Samir: For our most critical route, we want <100ms p95 and <250ms p99. Any rules of thumb on GPU counts for that?
[09:41] Maya: With average sequence lengths and a warmed KV cache, 1 A100-class GPU can serve X qps at <100ms p95 for model size Y—Diego will produce a simulation graph. But you'd need multiple GPUs for redundancy and to cover patch windows.
[09:56] Diego: I'll produce a sensitivity table: varying qps, sequence length, and warm/cold cache states to expected p95/p99.
[10:03] 
[10:20] Carlos: One concern is cold-starts—when a pool scales from zero. How is stateful KV cache populated on scale-up?
[10:28] Diego: Cold-starts are tricky. We have three levers: 1) proactive prewarm (start a container and run warmup script), 2) lazy fill (gradual KV population as requests hit), and 3) snapshot restore (persisted KV snapshot that can be loaded on container start). The snapshot is most effective if your workload has repeatable prefixes.
[10:48] Samir: Snapshot restore seems promising. Does it add start latency?
[10:52] Priya: There's an IO cost, but we stream snapshot restores in the background while the model accepts low-priority requests. You can also use a hybrid: restore hot keys first (top N prefixes) and background the rest.
[11:08] 
[11:26] Nadia: On encryption: are KV snapshots encrypted at rest and in transit? We must meet our SOC2 controls.
[11:31] Maya: Yes, encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private. Transit is mTLS. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO packet.
[11:42] 
[11:58] Diego: A practical micro-simulation we showed on screen (shared deck link: https://redwood.example/sim/polaris-tail-sim) — the key takeaway is that for heavy-tailed arrivals the marginal benefit of an extra reserved GPU drops quickly. Combining a modest reserved baseline with a fast fallback chain and KV warmup gives better cost/latency tradeoff.
[12:20] Samir: That link was helpful. Can you share a copy with our logs overlaid?
[12:25] Diego: Yes, please send traces to infra@redwood.example and we'll overlay.
[12:30] 
[12:45] Carlos: What about open-source runtime optimization like flash-attention variants—do you support those kernels or do you pick vendor-specific ones?
[12:52] Diego: We have a kernel registry. We evaluate community kernels like FlashAttention and vendor ones; the runtime picks at load time based on shape and measured throughput. Sometimes community kernels offer latency wins for specific shapes, but we validate accuracy and memory behavior first.
[13:10] Samir: How do you surface those runtime choices to customers?
[13:13] Maya: We include a per-route kernel selection log and performance fingerprint in the Console; you can export for audits.
[13:21] 
[13:33] Laura: For on-prem, are there limitations on autoscale (i.e., can it use cloud ephemeral GPUs)?
[13:40] Priya: On-prem Private cannot burst to Redwood-hosted GPUs by default because of network and tenancy separation. We can offer a hybrid contract where your Private cluster peeks into our burst pool over a VPN—requires negotiation and egress allowances.
[13:56] Samir: That hybrid option would be interesting—particularly for holiday spikes.
[14:01] Maya: We'll include hybrid burst terms in the pricing doc.
[14:09] 
[14:25] Diego: A few gotchas we often see: 1) frequent model swaps causing KV churn; 2) client-side fanouts where one external request spawns many sub-requests; 3) mismatched timeouts causing leaked workers. Monitoring for worker leaks and per-request token accounting helps.
[14:45] Carlos: On timeouts—what timeout pattern do you recommend end-to-end?
[14:49] Diego: Client timeout > internal route timeout + buffer. E.g., if route timeout is 300ms, client timeout 350–400ms to allow retries and fallbacks. Also use idempotent tokens for retries to avoid double-charging your quota.
[15:03] 
[15:20] Maya: Let's capture next steps and owners. Diego: build warmup + k6 script; Maya: pricing + capacity plan; Polaris: share traces and confirm dates for on-prem test. Anything else?
[15:33] Samir: We'll validate internal compliance checklist and send the audit-relevant fields.
[15:37] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the on-prem test slot and the security packet.
